r450: Being a good leader means being kind and clear, not being bossy or trying to make everyone like you.
r451: When a Son Stops Respecting His Father
r452: Rajesh, 46, engineer in Pune, father of fifteen-year-old Aarav
r453: Rajesh Kulkarni, an engineer in Pune, used to be his son Aarav's hero. Now fifteen, Aarav rolls his eyes, answers in one word and recently called him "a useless old man" in front of guests. Rajesh grew up in a home where talking back meant a slap, and he felt the same anger rise in him. He shouted, took away the phone for a month and refused to speak to Aarav for three days. The house went cold. Aarav's mother tried to make peace and ended up arguing with both of them. Rajesh felt humiliated and confused. "I give him everything," he told a friend at church, "and this is what I get?" Underneath, he felt a deep fear that he was losing his son.
r454: The teenage brain is under construction. Research suggests the emotional and reward systems mature earlier than the prefrontal cortex, which handles self-control and seeing other viewpoints. Teenagers also need to separate a little from parents to form their own identity, and that can come out clumsily as disrespect. For Rajesh, Aarav's words hit an old wound. His own father ruled through fear, and he had promised himself he would be different. When his son mocked him, his alarm system read it as both a challenge to his authority and proof that he had failed as a father. That double threat made him react harder than he wanted to.
r455: In a calm moment Rajesh realised he wanted his son's heart, not just his obedience. He asked himself, "What does Aarav need from me that he cannot say?" He decided to stop fighting for respect and start rebuilding connection, while still keeping clear limits.
r456: Calm down first and never correct his son in front of others
r457: Apologise for his own shouting and silent treatment
r458: Have a private respect conversation with one clear limit
r459: Spend fifteen minutes a day doing something Aarav enjoys
r460: Keep consequences calm, short and related to the behaviour
r461: Bless his son out loud for something good each week
r462: Scripture calls children to "Honour thy father and thy mother" (Exodus 20:12), but it also speaks directly to fathers: "Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). Authority in God's family is meant to be gentle, not crushing. In the parable of the prodigal son, the father did not chase respect. He waited, watched, ran and embraced his son (Luke 15:20). The son's disrespect was real, but the father's love was greater. Proverbs reminds us that "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1). And God disciplines us as a loving Father, always for our good (Hebrews 12:10).
r463: God designed families so that children grow from dependence to independence, and adolescence is the bridge between the two. Teenagers are wired to push away a little so they can become themselves. But their brains still borrow calm from steady adults. When a parent stays regulated, the teen's alarm system tends to settle too. God also designed relationships to heal through repair. Each time a parent apologises and reconnects, the child learns that love survives conflict. That learning builds trust and, in time, real respect.
r464: Colossians 3:21|Fathers, provoke not your children to anger, lest they be discouraged.
r468: Aarav did not change overnight. He laughed at his father's first apology. But Rajesh kept showing up, teaching him to drive on Sunday mornings. Three months later Aarav apologised on his own for a rude comment, mumbling it while looking at his phone. They still clash about screen time. But the house is warm again, and Aarav has started asking his father for advice.
r469: A father wins a teenager's respect by staying calm, repairing his own mistakes and keeping connection alive.
r470: When kids are rude, a good dad stays calm, says sorry when he gets angry and keeps loving them.
r471: The Class That Would Not Listen
r472: Grace, 38, English teacher of a class eight section in Shillong
r473: Grace Lyngdoh teaches English to class eight at a school in Shillong. One section, 8C, has become impossible. Students talk while she teaches, throw paper, and a few openly laugh when she gives instructions. One boy, Kevin, told her, "You can't do anything to us." Grace began dreading Tuesdays and Thursdays. She tried shouting, which worked for five minutes. She tried threats, which the class saw through. By the end of term she was crying in the staff toilet and wondering if she should quit teaching altogether. She felt like a failure, especially because her other classes loved her. At home she lay awake rehearsing angry speeches she would never give.
r474: A noisy, defiant classroom is a group nervous system. When a teacher is anxious, students sense it quickly, often without knowing they do. Research on co-regulation suggests that calm adults help calm children, and stressed adults can unintentionally raise the stress in a room. Many of Grace's students also had hard home lives. Kevin's father had recently left, and defiance was his way of feeling powerful when he felt powerless. For Grace, being mocked stirred old memories of being teased at school. Her alarm system made her either too loud or too quiet, and the class read both as weakness.
r475: An older teacher watched her class and said, "They are not testing your volume. They are testing whether you are safe and steady." Grace decided to lead from calm instead of fear, and to build relationships with the hardest students first.
r476: Breathe slowly and stand still before speaking to the class
r477: Agree three simple rules with the students and display them
r478: Speak to Kevin privately, with curiosity instead of threats
r479: Praise good behaviour quickly and specifically
r480: Follow through calmly on consequences every single time
r481: Pray for each student by name once a week
r482: Jesus taught crowds who were often restless, sceptical or hostile. Yet "the common people heard him gladly" (Mark 12:37), because He taught with authority and compassion together. When His own disciples argued about who was greatest, He set a child in the middle and taught them gently (Mark 9:36). Scripture says, "the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient" (2 Timothy 2:24). Gentleness is not weakness. Proverbs observes that "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty" (Proverbs 16:32). A steady teacher reflects the steady heart of God, who is "longsuffering to us-ward" (2 Peter 3:9).
r483: God designed human brains to learn best when they feel safe. A frightened or angry brain shifts into survival mode and stops absorbing new information. When a teacher stays calm, uses a lower voice and keeps predictable routines, students' threat systems settle and their thinking brains can engage. God also wired us to respond to warmth. A child who feels seen by one adult often starts to cooperate, because connection opens the door to correction. Calm authority mirrors God's own steady, patient leadership of us.
r484: 2 Timothy 2:24|And the servant of the Lord must not strive, but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient.
r488: 8C did not become a perfect class. Some days still went badly, and Grace had to involve the principal twice. But Kevin started staying after class to talk, and later helped her settle the others. Within two months the noise level dropped noticeably. Grace stopped dreading Tuesdays. She now mentors new teachers on leading from calm.
r489: Children follow a leader who is calm, consistent and kind far more than one who is loud.
r490: Kids listen better to a teacher who stays calm and kind than to one who shouts.
r492: Divya, 27, daughter-in-law in a joint family in Madurai
r493: Divya married into a joint family in Madurai two years ago. Her mother-in-law criticises her cooking in front of relatives, comments on her dark skin, and recently said, "Your mother never taught you anything." Divya's husband, Karthik, loves her but avoids conflict and says, "She is old, just adjust." Divya swallows the words, smiles, and cries in the bathroom later. Some nights she imagines shouting back. Other nights she wonders if her mother-in-law is right about her. She has started getting headaches, losing her appetite and avoiding the kitchen when others are there. She prays for patience but feels it running out. "I am becoming a person I do not recognise," she tells a friend on the phone.
r494: Repeated insults, especially from someone with power over us, keep the stress response switched on. Over time, research suggests, chronic stress can show up in the body as headaches, poor sleep and stomach trouble. Divya was raised to respect elders at any cost, so she swallowed her hurt. But swallowed words do not disappear. They often turn into resentment, shame or illness. Her mother-in-law, it later emerged, had been treated harshly as a young bride herself, and was repeating what she had received. Hurt people often hurt people, though that never makes it acceptable.
r495: Divya learned the difference between retaliating, absorbing and responding. She did not have to choose between shouting and silence. She could respond calmly, bless instead of curse, and still set a clear limit, with her husband standing beside her.
r496: Pause and breathe before answering any insult
r497: Tell Karthik privately how it hurts and ask him to stand with her
r498: Answer insults with one short, calm and respectful sentence
r499: Refuse to insult back and pray a blessing for her mother-in-law
r500: Spend time each week outside the house with friends or church
r501: Seek a counsellor or pastor if the insults continue or worsen
r502: Scripture does not ask us to pretend insults do not hurt. David wrote, "For it was not an enemy that reproached me, then I could have borne it" (Psalm 55:12). Pain from people close to us cuts deep. Yet Jesus taught, "Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you" (Luke 6:28). Peter wrote that Jesus, "when he was reviled, reviled not again" but "committed himself to him that judgeth righteously" (1 Peter 2:23). Blessing is not the same as accepting mistreatment. Scripture also says a man shall "leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife" (Genesis 2:24), protecting his marriage.
r503: God designed us with an alarm system to protect us, and with a thinking brain that can choose a response. A short pause and a slow breath help the body move from reacting to responding. Blessing someone who has hurt us also changes our own brain. Research on compassion practices suggests they can reduce bitterness and calm stress. God created marriage as a protected bond, so a spouse's support powerfully lowers stress. Healthy boundaries and blessing together protect both the heart and the relationship.
r504: Luke 6:28|Bless them that curse you, and pray for them which despitefully use you.
r508: Karthik was slow to act, but after a counselling session at church he spoke gently and clearly to his mother. The insults reduced, though they did not stop. Divya now answers calmly, "Amma, please do not speak about my mother like that." Twice her mother-in-law apologised. Divya's headaches come less often. She still has hard days, but she no longer feels she is disappearing.
r509: You can answer insults with calm, blessing and clear limits instead of swallowing them or hitting back.
r510: When someone says mean things, you can stay calm, say kindly that it is not okay and ask God to bless them.
r511: Shouted At in Front of Everyone
r512: Joseph, 34, sales executive in Mumbai with a baby on the way
r513: Joseph D'Souza works in sales for a company in Mumbai. In a team meeting his manager shouted at him for missing a target, calling him "lazy" and "a joke" in front of twelve colleagues. Joseph's face went hot and his mind went blank. He could not say anything. Afterwards he sat in the parking lot shaking. That night he replayed the scene again and again, imagining comebacks. For the next week he avoided his manager, felt sick on the train each morning and made more mistakes than usual. He started to believe he really was useless. He thought of quitting, but he has a home loan and a baby on the way.
r514: Public humiliation is one of the strongest social threats a person can face. When Joseph was shouted at, his brain likely went into a freeze response. Attention shifted toward survival, and the thinking and speaking parts of the brain seemed to go offline, which is why his mind went blank. Afterwards, the brain's default mode network kept replaying the scene, trying to make sense of the danger. Joseph also had a history. A headmaster once humiliated him in front of the whole school assembly. The new insult woke the old shame, making the manager's words feel like the truth about him rather than one man's anger.
r515: His pastor told him, "His words described his anger, not your identity." Joseph decided to regulate first, then reflect honestly on any real feedback, and then respond with dignity instead of hiding or exploding.
r516: Use slow breathing on the train to calm the body each morning
r517: Write down the insult and separate fact from accusation
r518: Ask for a private meeting and calmly request respectful feedback
r519: Fix the real sales problem with a clear plan
r520: Pray a blessing for his manager instead of rehearsing revenge
r521: Report repeated abuse to HR in writing if it continues
r522: Jesus was publicly mocked, spat upon and insulted, yet He did not lose His identity. Isaiah foretold, "I hid not my face from shame and spitting. For the Lord GOD will help me, therefore shall I not be confounded" (Isaiah 50:6-7). Scripture tells us to answer wisely, not harshly: "A soft answer turneth away wrath" (Proverbs 15:1). Paul urged, "Recompense to no man evil for evil" (Romans 12:17). And God promises that "every tongue that shall rise against thee in judgment thou shalt condemn" (Isaiah 54:17). Our worth is set by God, not by a boss's anger. We can accept fair correction and still refuse false labels.
